## Engineering principles

Practices for all work in this repository, from *Software Engineering: Standing on the
Shoulders of Giants* (<https://www.swebook.org>). Section references point at the chapter
that explains the *why* — read it before arguing with a rule here.

$project_context

### How to approach any change

1. **Know what you are building before you build it.** Restate the requirement as a
   testable statement. If you cannot say how you would check it, you do not yet have a
   requirement — you have a wish (Ch. 3).
2. **Make the smallest change that delivers the value.** Slice work so something works
   end-to-end early, then deepen it. A thin slice that runs beats a broad one that does
   not (Ch. 2; the walking skeleton, App. A).
3. **Leave the code better than you found it.** Fix the small thing you noticed on the way
   past — repository stewardship is a practice, not a cleanup sprint (§15.4).
4. **Do not add what was not asked for.** No speculative abstractions, no error handling
   for conditions that cannot occur, no refactoring bundled into a feature commit. Trust
   internal invariants; validate at system boundaries (Ch. 6).

### Requirements and acceptance criteria (Ch. 3–5)

- Write the need from the user's side before writing code:
  **As a `<role>`, I want `<capability>`, so that `<benefit>`** (Connextra form, §3.3).
- Every story carries **acceptance criteria** that a test can check. "Works correctly" is
  not a criterion; "returns 401 for an expired token" is.
- Apply **INVEST** — independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small, testable. A story
  failing *testable* or *small* gets split before work starts.
- For non-trivial user-facing behavior, model the flow as a **use case** with its main
  success scenario and the extensions that matter (Ch. 5). The extensions are usually where
  the defects live.
- Ask what must *not* happen. Threats and abuse cases are requirements too (§3.7).

### Behavior-driven development (Ch. 3, Ch. 10)

- Express acceptance criteria as **Given / When / Then** scenarios in the language of the
  domain, not the implementation. `Given an expired session` — never
  `Given the session_expiry column is in the past`.
- The scenario is the shared artifact: it is a requirement, a conversation, and an
  executable test at once. When a scenario and the code disagree, decide which is wrong —
  do not silently edit the scenario to match the code.
- Keep scenarios declarative. One behavior each; no UI mechanics, no test-data setup
  bleeding into the narrative.
- **Automate them.** A scenario nobody runs is documentation that will drift. Wire them
  into $test_cmd and let CI run them.

### Test-driven development (Ch. 10)

- **Red → green → refactor.** Write a failing test, *watch it fail*, make it pass with the
  simplest change that works, then refactor with the test as your safety net.
- **Never trust a test you have never seen fail.** After writing an assertion, break the
  code or invert the expectation once and confirm the test goes red. A test that has only
  ever been green is not yet evidence — it may be asserting nothing (§10.1.5).
- **Pick the oracle deliberately** — exact value, property, or cross-check against a
  trusted implementation. Most weak tests are weak because nobody chose how they would
  know the answer was right (§10.2).
- Test **behavior, not implementation**. A test that breaks on every refactor is testing
  the wrong thing.
- Cover the **failure paths**: empty input, boundary values, expired or malformed data,
  the dependency being down. Happy-path-only suites report high coverage and catch little.
- Work at more than one level — fast unit tests for logic, integration tests for the seams
  where components meet, a thin layer of end-to-end tests for the critical journeys.
- **Coverage measures execution, not verification.** Use it to find untested code, never as
  a target to hit (Ch. 12 on why targets corrupt metrics).
- Fix or delete flaky tests immediately. A suite people have learned to re-run is a suite
  that no longer gates anything.
- Bug fixes start with a **failing regression test** that reproduces the bug. Then fix it.

### Design and architecture (Ch. 6–7)

- Aim for **high cohesion, low coupling**. A module should do one thing; changing it should
  not require reading everything else.
- Watch file and function size as a proxy for cohesion. When one file starts attracting
  every change, that is the signal to extract, not a reason to scroll faster.
- Choose a known pattern deliberately and apply it consistently; a half-applied pattern is
  worse than none (Ch. 7).
- Record decisions that were expensive to make as **ADRs** in `docs/adr/` — context,
  decision, consequences. Future maintainers need the *why*, which the code cannot carry.
- Prefer changing structure incrementally behind working tests (**strangler fig**) over
  rewrites (§15.6).

### Version control (Ch. 8)

- **Small, focused commits.** One logical change each; never bundle a refactor with a
  feature.
- Write messages that answer "why", not "what" — the diff already says what. Use
  **Conventional Commits**: `feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`, `refactor:`, `test:`, `chore:`.
- Branch per unit of work; open a pull request; get a review before merging to the main
  branch. Review is a defect-removal technique, not a formality (§9.2).
- **Never commit secrets.** No `.env`, no keys, no tokens, no `master.key`. Add them to
  `.gitignore` *before* the first commit — an ignore rule added later does not untrack a
  file that is already in history.
- Never rewrite shared history as a default team policy; when it is genuinely necessary
  (a leaked secret), tell everyone first.

### Static checking (Ch. 9)

- Run a **linter**, a **formatter**, and — where the language supports it — a **type
  checker**. Configure them once, commit the config, and let CI enforce them.
- Fix warnings or explicitly suppress them with a reason. A build with 400 warnings has no
  warnings.
- Static analysis catches whole classes of defect before a test runs, and it is the
  cheapest check you own (§9.4).$lint_note

### Security (Ch. 11)

- **Secrets come from the environment**, never from source. Commit a `.env.example` with
  the key names and no values.
- Validate and sanitize at every trust boundary. Parameterize queries; never build SQL,
  shell commands, or file paths by string concatenation.
- **Pin dependencies with a lockfile** and keep them updated — enable Dependabot or
  Renovate. Most breaches arrive through a dependency, not your code (§11.5).
- Run dependency scanning (SCA) and static security analysis (SAST) in CI.
- Treat the OWASP Top 10 as a review checklist for anything handling untrusted input.
- Fail closed: on error, deny access rather than allowing it.

### Delivery (Ch. 14)

- **CI on every push**: build, lint, test. A check that cannot fail the build is a
  notification, not a gate — no `continue-on-error` on anything you rely on.
- Keep the main branch releasable. If it is broken, fixing it is the team's top priority.
- **Config from the environment**, one build artifact promoted across environments
  (twelve-factor). Never a separate build per environment.
- Make setup reproducible from a clean clone — a container, a lockfile, and a README that
  actually works. Test it by following your own instructions.
- Track the **DORA metrics** as a set of five: change lead time, deployment frequency,
  failed-deployment recovery time, change fail rate, and deployment rework rate. Speed and
  stability are read together or not at all.

### Metrics (Ch. 12)

- Measure to answer a **question**, not to fill a dashboard (Goal–Question–Metric).
- Any metric adopted as a target stops measuring what it measured. Watch trends; do not
  set quotas on coverage, velocity, or commit counts.
- Small samples lie. Two data points are not a trend.

### Maintenance and evolution (Ch. 15)

- Before changing code you do not understand, put a **characterization test** around the
  current behavior so you can tell a change from a break.
- Track technical debt explicitly — an issue with a cost and a trigger, not a `TODO` that
  will outlive the team.
- Keep documentation next to the thing it documents, and update it in the same commit.
  Docs that contradict the code are worse than no docs.

### Working with AI assistance (Ch. 13)

- **You own everything you merge.** Generated code gets the same review, tests, and static
  checks as hand-written code — no exceptions, no fast path.
- Generation moves effort to **verification**; it does not remove it. Budget the time you
  saved for reading the diff carefully.
- Ask for a failing test alongside any generated fix, and confirm it fails before the fix
  is applied.
- Be suspicious of confident code touching security, concurrency, money, or time zones —
  the places where plausible and correct diverge most.
- Keep this file current. It is the durable context that makes the next session useful;
  a stale `CLAUDE.md` actively misleads.

### Definition of done

A change is done when all of these hold — not when the code works on your machine:

- [ ] Acceptance criteria met and demonstrable
- [ ] Tests written, seen to fail, now passing — including a failure-path case
- [ ] Lint, format, and type checks clean
- [ ] No secrets, no debug output, no commented-out code
- [ ] Reviewed by someone who did not write it
- [ ] Docs and this file updated if behavior or setup changed
- [ ] CI green on the branch

> Score this repository against these practices at any time: see the `repo-scorecard`
> skill, or Appendix A §A.6 of the book.
